title: You Can Sing to God and Still Hide From Him — The Deeper Meaning of John 4:24
paragraphs: You Can Sing to God and Still Hide From Him — The Deeper Meaning of John 4:24
Jesus said the Father is looking for worshipers “in spirit and truth.” But He said it to a woman carrying a history she probably wished nobody knew. That changes everything.
There is something frightening about realizing that you can be standing in a place of worship and still be hiding from God.
You can know the songs.
You can raise your hands.
You can say “Amen” at exactly the right moment.
You can post the Bible verse.

You can serve in church, encourage everybody else, tell people that God is good—and then go home carrying a secret life, a wounded heart, an unforgiven grudge, an addiction nobody knows about, a relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ, or a private emptiness you have learned to cover with Christian language.
And perhaps that is why John 4:24 is much more unsettling—and much more beautiful—than many of us realize.
Jesus says:
“God is Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship in spirit and truth.”
The Greek text reads:
πνεῦμα ὁ θεός, καὶ τοὺς προσκυνοῦντας αὐτὸν ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ δεῖ προσκυνεῖν.
Pneuma ho Theos, kai tous proskynountas auton en pneumati kai alētheia dei proskynein.
God is Spirit, and those worshiping Him must worship in spirit and truth.
But here is what we often miss.
Jesus did not say these words from a stage.
He did not deliver them inside the Jerusalem temple.
There was no worship band.
No congregation.
No religious atmosphere.
There was a well.
There was a thirsty woman.
There was a complicated past.
And there was Jesus.
That matters.
Because John 4:24 is not merely Jesus giving us instructions about how to conduct a worship service.
It is part of an encounter in which Jesus is tearing down the hiding places of the human heart while simultaneously offering grace to the person hiding inside them.
The woman of Samaria had come to draw water, but Jesus began talking about a thirst no bucket could satisfy.
He offered her “living water.”
Then the conversation became painfully personal.
Jesus told her to call her husband.
She answered that she had no husband.
Jesus already knew.
He knew that she had had five husbands and that the man currently in her life was not her husband.
Imagine the silence after that.
Imagine having your carefully edited biography opened by a stranger beside a well.
Imagine realizing that the Man asking you for water already knows the chapters you hoped would remain unread.
Yet notice what Jesus does not do.
He does not walk away.
He does not treat her as contaminated.
He does not pretend her sin and brokenness are irrelevant either.
Grace does not require Jesus to lie about us.
Grace means He can tell us the truth about us and still invite us to Himself.
That is the Gospel.

Some of us have confused grace with God refusing to confront what is destroying us. But biblical grace does something far more wonderful. Jesus brings the darkness into the light because He intends redemption, not because He enjoys humiliation.
The woman then raises the centuries-old dispute about worship. Her Samaritan ancestors worshiped on their mountain; the Jews maintained that Jerusalem was the proper place.
Which mountain?
Which location?
Which religious tradition?
And Jesus takes the conversation somewhere deeper.
The hour is coming—and has arrived—when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.
Then comes the sentence:
πνεῦμα ὁ θεός.
Pneuma ho Theos.
God is Spirit.

The Greek word pneuma can carry the sense of spirit, breath, or wind depending upon context. Here Jesus is speaking about the nature of God. God is not confined by the geographical boundaries human beings try to place around Him.
He cannot be reduced to a mountain.
He cannot be contained inside a building.
He cannot be manipulated by ritual.
The God who is Spirit requires worship appropriate to who He truly is.
That means Christianity can never ultimately be reduced to “I went to church.”
You can enter a church building without surrendering your heart.
You can sing without adoring.
You can kneel while inwardly resisting God.
You can know Christian vocabulary without knowing Christ.
You can appear spiritually alive before people while being spiritually cold before God.
Jesus is moving the woman away from the question, “Where is the correct place?” toward the far more penetrating question:
“What kind of worshiper is the Father seeking?”
And John has already given us the answer immediately before verse 24.
The Father seeks true worshipers.
Think about that.
The Father is seeking.
Not flawless performers.
Not religious celebrities.
Not people who have successfully hidden every embarrassing chapter of their lives.
Worshipers.
And the woman standing before Jesus has a history.
That is where this becomes personal.
Maybe your history is not hers.
Maybe nobody would call your life scandalous.
But perhaps you know what it is to smile while breaking inside.
Perhaps you know how exhausting it is to maintain a version of yourself for everybody else.
Perhaps there is something you desperately hope never becomes public.
Something you did.
Something done to you.
Something you keep returning to.
Something you cannot seem to forgive.
Something you promised God you would stop.
Something you deleted from your phone but not from your heart.
And sometimes we do exactly what the Samaritan woman did.
When Jesus gets close to the wound, we change the subject to religion.
We debate theology while avoiding repentance.
We discuss churches while avoiding surrender.
We argue about worship styles while withholding worship.
We can become experts at discussing God precisely because discussing God feels safer than being exposed before Him.
But Jesus keeps going deeper.
He says worship must happen ἐν πνεύματι καὶ ἀληθείᾳ—en pneumati kai alētheia—“in spirit and truth.”
The word alētheia means truth, reality, what is true rather than falsehood.
This destroys performance Christianity.
Truth means I stop presenting God with the edited version of myself.
Truth means the mask comes off.
Truth means I stop calling bondage “just a struggle” when God is calling me to repentance.
Truth means I stop calling bitterness “discernment.”
Truth means I stop calling pride “standards.”
Truth means I stop calling lust “loneliness.”
Truth means I stop calling disobedience “my personal journey.”
Truth means I stop pretending that outward Christianity can substitute for inward surrender.
But truth also means something even greater.
Christian worship is not merely being sincere.
A person can be sincerely wrong.
Jesus Himself says in this conversation that salvation is from the Jews, and moments later He identifies Himself to the woman as the Messiah.
Truth therefore cannot be separated from Christ.
Later in John's Gospel, Jesus declares that He is “the way, and the truth, and the life.”
So worship in truth is not “whatever feels authentic to me.”
The center of Christian worship is not the worshiper.
It is God as He truly is, supremely revealed in Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters enormously in a culture that often treats sincerity as the highest spiritual authority.
Jesus does not say, “As long as you mean it, everything is worship.”
He says the Father seeks worshipers in spirit and truth.
And there is another small Greek word in John 4:24 that should stop us.
δεῖ.
Dei.
It means “it is necessary,” “one must,” “it is required.”
Jesus does not present spirit and truth as optional upgrades for unusually serious Christians.
Those who worship God must worship this way.
Not because God is impressed by our spiritual intensity.
Because worship must correspond to the God being worshiped.
God is Spirit.
God is true.
Therefore genuine worship cannot finally be reduced to location, ritual, appearance, music, emotion, denomination, or religious performance.
It must become real.
This does not mean emotions are bad.
It does not mean singing is unimportant.
It does not mean gathering as the church is optional.
It does not mean doctrine alone constitutes worship.
It means something much more searching.
God wants you.
Not the church version of you.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the Sunday version.
Not the version that knows when to raise its hands.
You.
Your heart.
Your allegiance.
Your repentance.
Your trust.
Your obedience.
Your wounds.
Your gratitude.
Your shame brought into His light.
Your whole life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And this is where the story at the well becomes breathtaking.
Because the woman eventually says that she knows Messiah is coming.
Jesus answers her.
The One speaking to her is He.
The conversation about worship ultimately leads to the Worshiper standing face-to-face with the One worthy of worship.
She came looking for water.
She encountered Messiah.
She arrived carrying a jar.
She left carrying testimony.
John tells us that she left her water jar and went back to the town.
Do not rush past that abandoned jar.
The thing she came for was suddenly no longer the biggest thing in her life.
She tells the people:
Come see a Man who told me what I have done.
Think about the astonishing transformation contained in that invitation.
The very history that might once have made her hide becomes part of the testimony that points people toward Jesus.
That is grace.
Jesus knew.
Jesus stayed.
Jesus spoke truth.
Jesus revealed Himself.
And she went back.
This is why our message at Gospel Warrior continues to be:
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because grace calls sin good.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus rewrites everything because the Gospel takes what sin meant for destruction and brings the sinner into forgiveness, reconciliation, holiness, and new life through Christ.
The cross proves that God does not save us by ignoring sin.
He saves sinners because Jesus bears sin.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is not God lowering His holiness until our rebellion no longer matters.
Forgiveness was purchased at immeasurable cost.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from the thing killing you toward the Savior who gives life.
Maybe this article found you while you are tired of pretending.
Maybe nobody knows what has been happening inside you.
Maybe your worship has become mechanical.
Maybe you sing about surrender while secretly negotiating which parts of your life Jesus is allowed to touch.
Maybe you have confused tears with transformation.
Maybe you have confused church attendance with communion with Christ.
Maybe you have spent years protecting a reputation while your soul slowly starved.
Then hear John 4 again.
The Father is seeking worshipers.
And the Christ who met a broken woman beside a well still receives sinners who come to Him.
You do not need a cleaner past before coming to Jesus.
You need Jesus to redeem your past and rule your present.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the question you are afraid to ask.
Bring Him the failure you keep replaying at three in the morning.
Stop trying to impress the One who already knows.
That may be one of the most liberating truths in this entire story:
Jesus knew before she confessed.
And He stayed.
He knew before she understood who He was.
And He stayed.
He knew the names.
The relationships.
The failures.
The thirst beneath the thirst.
And He stayed.
If that exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop hiding from God.
Not as a superstition.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Send it privately to the person who has stopped going to church.

Supporting faithful Gospel work can itself be an act of Christian generosity and partnership when it flows from love for Christ—not a payment to God, not a requirement for salvation, and not a measure of someone's faithfulness.
Because there may come a night when worship feels empty and you need to remember what Jesus actually said.
Worship is not hiding behind a song.
It is not finding the perfect building.
It is not manufacturing an emotional moment.

It is coming before the Father through Christ with a heart awakened to God, refusing falsehood, surrendering to His truth, and allowing the Gospel to reach the places we spent years trying to conceal.
Because somewhere, even now, somebody is still walking toward a well carrying a jar they believe will finally satisfy them.
Another relationship.
Another achievement.
Another purchase.
Another distraction.
Another secret habit.
Another attempt to feel wanted.
Another Sunday of pretending.
And Jesus is already there.
He knows why you came.
He knows what you have done.
He knows what happened to you.
He knows what you are hiding.
He knows what you are thirsty for.
And He is still offering living water.
The woman came to the well carrying the evidence of her thirst; she left carrying the name of the One who finally knew how to satisfy it.
